question: Tell me about a time your team argued about what the customer wanted without any evidence. How did you settle it?

raiseTranscript.text: Our team was split on whether customers wanted a simpler onboarding flow or more tutorial videos. I suggested we pull support tickets and run a quick 5-user test instead of debating.
I owned pulling the last 30 tickets and shared a one-page summary. The data showed 70% dropped at the first step due to unclear labels. We shipped the simpler flow and saw activation up 12%.
How did the team react to your suggestion?
One engineer pushed back at first, but after seeing the tickets they agreed. I learned to bring a small artifact early rather than argue.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team argued about what the customer wanted without any evidence. How did you settle it?
Candidate pulled support tickets and ran 5-user test on own initiative
Quote: 'I learned to bring a small artifact early rather than argue'
Follow-up: Asked how team reacted; candidate owned the follow-through and noted coachability on bringing data sooner
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Wow the Customer for a junior. The candidate moved from opinion debate to pulling tickets and running a small test without waiting for permission. Quote shows they owned the artifact creation and later reflected on bringing data earlier. This matches junior scope where individual initiative and learning from the outcome matter most. The 12% activation lift is local but concrete. Biggest strength is shifting the team from argument to evidence with minimal process.

lowerTranscript.text: We kept going back and forth on whether customers needed more features or a cleaner UI. I thought cleaner UI made sense from my own experience.
Did anyone suggest looking at data?
Not really, we just voted and went with the majority view. Later the feature usage was low but we didn't revisit it.

At junior level this shows limited ownership of moving the team to customer signals. Biggest gap is defaulting to consensus instead of seeking observable customer behavior.

raiseTranscript.text: Two squads disagreed on whether enterprise customers wanted deeper integrations or faster self-serve setup. I organized a joint review of win-loss notes and ran three customer calls with the account team.
How did you get buy-in across squads?
I shared anonymized call clips and a simple table of requests vs current gaps. Both squads aligned on prioritizing self-serve improvements first.
Self-serve conversion rose 18% in the next quarter and the other squad later reused the call format on their own roadmap.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team argued about what the customer wanted without any evidence. How did you settle it?

Shared clips and gap table to align teams without authority
Outcome: 18% self-serve conversion lift; other squad adopted the format
Follow-up: Asked about buy-in; candidate used artifacts to influence without mandate
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Wow the Customer for a senior. The candidate used existing win-loss notes and ran targeted calls to replace debate with shared evidence across two squads. Influence came through artifacts rather than authority. The 18% lift is tied to the decision and the practice spread to another team. This shows the expected cross-team scope and raising the bar on how decisions are made. Biggest strength is turning a disagreement into reusable customer insight process.

I suggested we decide in the next planning meeting. We ended up splitting the difference and building a bit of both.

raiseTranscript.text: Two product lines were locked in a roadmap debate about whether customers valued breadth of integrations or depth in core workflows. I commissioned a quarterly customer research cadence and required both teams to reference the same dataset before any prioritization discussion.

We delayed two integration projects by a quarter to fund the research program. The first round showed depth mattered more for retention, so we redirected investment and saw net revenue retention improve 7 points over 18 months.
How did this change org behavior?
Other directors started requiring the same research link in their PRDs. We later embedded a small research budget into every major initiative.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team argued about what the customer wanted without any evidence. How did you settle it?

Trade-off: delayed integrations to fund research; NRR +7 pts over 18 months
Quote on spreading practice: 'Other directors started requiring the same research link'
Follow-up: Asked about trade-offs and org change; candidate showed long-term leverage
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Wow the Customer at exec level. The candidate addressed repeated cross-org debates by institutionalizing a shared research cadence instead of resolving one instance. The explicit trade-off of delaying projects to fund research demonstrates strategic judgment on where to spend leverage. The 7-point NRR lift over 18 months and adoption by other directors show durable org impact. This matches exec scope of creating systems that reduce future opinion-based arguments. Biggest strength is turning a recurring problem into a scalable decision filter.
